title: Vegan B12 Dosage Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Find the right B12 dosage for vegans. Get personalized daily, weekly, or monthly supplement recommendations based on current NIH and Vegan Society guidelines.
intro: Vitamin B12 is the one nutrient that every vegan must supplement — no plant food reliably provides it in absorbable quantities. This calculator applies the dosage schedules recommended by the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements and the Vegan Society: **25–100 mcg daily** or **2,000 mcg once a week**. Choose your preferred supplement frequency and get the correct target dose, the best form to take, and the monitoring schedule to confirm it's working.
keyTakeaway: B12 absorption is capped by intrinsic factor (~1.5–2 mcg per active-transport dose). Vegans must compensate with much higher supplemental doses: 25–100 mcg/day or 2,000 mcg/week of cyanocobalamin. Monthly dosing does not work — passive diffusion alone cannot meet the weekly requirement.
useCases: A new vegan who wants to know exactly how much B12 to buy and take from day one
A long-term vegan switching from daily to weekly dosing who wants to confirm the correct weekly amount
A dietitian or GP advising plant-based patients on evidence-based supplement schedules
A parent of a vegan child checking whether the adult schedule applies (it does not — see FAQ)

example.title: Worked Example — Weekly Dosing
steps: Intrinsic-factor active transport saturates at ~1.5–2 mcg per dose
Passive diffusion absorbs ~1% of an unbound oral dose
To deliver ≥16.8 mcg/day via passive diffusion once a week: 2,000 mcg × 1% ≈ 20 mcg absorbed per dose, spread over 7 days ≈ ~2.9 mcg/day — above the adult RDA of 2.4 mcg/day

explanation:
## Why vegans need supplemental B12

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is synthesised only by certain bacteria and archaea. It accumulates in animal tissues, making meat, fish, eggs and dairy the main dietary sources. Whole plant foods contain no reliably absorbable B12; fermented foods, algae and mushrooms provide amounts too small and variable to count on. Vegans who don't supplement consistently develop deficiency — sometimes years before symptoms appear — because the liver stores 2–5 mg of B12 and depletion is slow.

## How absorption works (and why it matters for dosing)

The gut absorbs B12 by two routes:

| Route | Mechanism | Capacity | When it applies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active transport | Intrinsic factor (IF) glycoprotein | ~1.5–2 mcg per dose | Low-dose supplements, food |
| Passive diffusion | Direct mucosal absorption | ~1% of dose, unlimited | High-dose supplements |

Because IF saturates rapidly, taking **2.4 mcg once a day** (the RDA for non-vegans eating B12-rich food) is nowhere near enough from a supplement alone. The supplemental doses must be high enough for passive diffusion to carry the rest.

## How it's calculated

This calculator applies the dosage schedules published by the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements and endorsed by the Vegan Society and VeganHealth.org:

- **Daily:** 25–100 mcg of cyanocobalamin. The lower end (~25 mcg) saturates IF and lets passive diffusion add ~0.25 mcg per day on top, comfortably exceeding the 2.4 mcg RDA. Going up to 100 mcg adds a safety margin for people with lower absorption.
- **Weekly:** 2,000 mcg in a single dose. At 1% passive diffusion: 2,000 × 0.01 = 20 mcg absorbed, divided over 7 days ≈ 2.9 mcg/day — above the RDA.
- **Monthly:** Not recommended. A single monthly mega-dose would require ~72,000 mcg to deliver 2.4 mcg/day via passive diffusion alone, which is impractical and untested. No established guideline supports monthly B12 oral supplementation.

## Cyanocobalamin vs. methylcobalamin

Cyanocobalamin is the standard recommendation for vegan supplementation because:
- It is the most chemically stable form (shelf-stable at room temperature)
- It has the largest evidence base from clinical trials
- It is the most cost-effective form
- The body readily converts it to methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin (the two active forms)

Methylcobalamin is bioactive without conversion, but is less stable, more expensive, and has fewer controlled trials in vegans. It is an acceptable alternative but not superior for most healthy adults.

## Reference blood values

| Biomarker | Normal range (adults) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Serum B12 | 200–900 pg/mL | Low sensitivity for functional deficiency |
| Holotranscobalamin (active B12) | >35 pmol/L | Earlier marker of depletion |
| Methylmalonic acid (MMA) | <0.4 μmol/L | Most sensitive functional marker |
| Homocysteine | <12 μmol/L | Elevated when B12 or folate is low |

> **Disclaimer:** This calculator is for educational reference only and does not replace personalised medical advice. If you have symptoms of deficiency (fatigue, tingling, anaemia, neurological changes) or abnormal blood results, consult a healthcare professional.

faq.q: Why is 2.4 mcg per day (the adult RDA) not enough for vegans to supplement with?
faq.a: The RDA assumes the body will absorb B12 from food via intrinsic factor across multiple small meals. A single supplement dose saturates intrinsic factor at about 1.5–2 mcg; anything above that relies on passive diffusion at only 1% efficiency. So a 2.4 mcg supplement pill delivers only about 1.7 mcg total — below the RDA. Supplements must be high-dose to compensate.

faq.q: Can I take 1,000 mcg of B12 every day instead of 2,000 mcg once a week?
faq.a: Yes. Taking 1,000 mcg daily delivers about 1,000 × 1% = 10 mcg by passive diffusion plus ~2 mcg via intrinsic factor ≈ 12 mcg/day — well above the RDA and a safe approach. This is often used by people recovering from deficiency or with malabsorption. The 25–100 mcg/day range given by this calculator is the minimum-effective approach for healthy vegans without deficiency.

To supply 2.4 mcg/day for 30 days via passive diffusion alone (≈72 mcg total absorbed), you would need a 7,200 mcg single dose — and no guideline recommends this because absorption efficiency, gut transit, and safety at that dose haven't been established in trials. Monthly injections of hydroxocobalamin are used medically, but that is a prescription treatment for pernicious anaemia, not oral supplementation.

faq.q: Is cyanocobalamin safe? It contains cyanide.
faq.a: Yes. The tiny amount of cyanide in a cyanocobalamin supplement (a few micrograms) is far below any toxicological threshold and is rapidly excreted. Heavy smokers may prefer methylcobalamin because their bodies already process more cyanide, but for non-smokers cyanocobalamin is equally safe and better studied. No tolerable upper intake level (UL) has been established for B12 because no adverse effects from high oral doses have been documented.

faq.q: What are the first signs of B12 deficiency?
faq.a: Early signs include fatigue, brain fog, and glossitis (sore, inflamed tongue). As deficiency deepens: macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, peripheral tingling or numbness (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord), and mood changes. Neurological damage can be irreversible if deficiency persists for years. Deficiency can take 3–5 years to become symptomatic because of liver stores, making preventive supplementation essential from the start of a vegan diet.

faq.q: Which blood tests should vegans get to monitor B12 status?
faq.a: Serum B12 alone is not reliable — it can look normal even when functional B12 is depleted. A complete B12 panel includes: (1) Serum B12, (2) Holotranscobalamin (active B12, the earliest marker of depletion), (3) Methylmalonic acid (MMA) — the most sensitive functional marker, and (4) Homocysteine. Ask your doctor to check all four if you suspect deficiency. Recheck every 6–12 months while on a stable supplement regimen.

faq.q: Do B12-fortified foods count toward the recommended intake?
faq.a: Yes, if consumed consistently. The Vegan Society recommends eating fortified foods 2–3 times a day to get at least 3 mcg of B12 daily from food (e.g., fortified plant milks, nutritional yeast, breakfast cereals). However, fortification levels vary by brand and country, and eating habits change — supplementation is more reliable and is the approach recommended by most vegan nutrition experts.

faq.q: Do vegan children need a different B12 dose?
faq.a: Yes. The RDA for B12 varies by age: 0.9 mcg/day (1–3 years), 1.2 mcg/day (4–8 years), 1.8 mcg/day (9–13 years), and 2.4 mcg/day (adults). Supplemental doses for children should be adjusted accordingly and ideally confirmed with a paediatrician or registered dietitian specialising in plant-based nutrition. This calculator is designed for adults only.

faq.q: Can pregnant or breastfeeding vegans use this calculator?
faq.a: Pregnant and lactating people have higher B12 needs (2.6 mcg/day and 2.8 mcg/day respectively per NIH). The dosage ranges in this calculator provide a safe margin above those levels, but if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning pregnancy on a vegan diet, consult a healthcare provider — they may recommend a higher or more closely monitored supplementation protocol.
